game/game: Here is a game. Read a text one letter at a time, and before each new letter, guess what it will be. After h, e, l, l, most people would guess o.
game/shannon: In 1951, Claude Shannon played this game with people, in a paper called Prediction and Entropy of Printed English. How well they guessed measured how predictable English is: its entropy, the average surprise per letter.
game/free: The game needs nobody to grade it. A classifier needs someone to label every image, cat or ship. Text holds its own answers: each letter is the right answer for the letters before it.
game/lm: So any text at all can teach a model to play. A model that plays is called a language model: a model of how a language goes, of which pieces tend to follow which.
game/vocab: The pieces it reads are tokens, here single characters. Its vocabulary, every token it knows, is just h, e, l and o, with ids zero to three. Its size, V, is four.
shift/inputs: Feed hello in, one character at a time. The inputs are h, e, l, l: every letter but the last, since nothing follows the o.
shift/shift: The targets are the same text, shifted by one place: e, l, l, o. Each step's target is the letter that comes next.
shift/y: Number the steps with t, from zero, and call step t's target y of t, written as its id. At step zero, after h, the target is e: id one.
shift/memory: Steps two and three both read an l, but one must predict l, and the other o. The input alone cannot tell them apart. The memory, h, can: it knows whether one l has come, or two.
guess/scores: At each step, the network reads its memory, h, through one more matrix of weights, W h y: hidden to output. Out comes one score for every token in the vocabulary.
guess/V: That is V scores, four here, however big the memory and however long the text: the next letter could be any token, so every token gets a score.
guess/softmax: Softmax turns the scores into probabilities for the next letter. After reading h, this model gives the target, e, zero point five.
guess/id: To find the target in p, use its id. e is token one, so its probability is entry one: p of one.
guess/every: Every step makes a guess like this, over the whole vocabulary, against its own target: the one bar that should be tall.
loss/step: Each guess is a classification over the vocabulary, so its loss, L of t, is cross-entropy: minus the log of the target's probability. At step zero, minus ln zero point five is zero point six nine.
loss/all: Every step pays for its own target the same way. The surer the guess, the less it pays: the last step, which gave its target zero point eight, pays only zero point two two.
loss/elman: Shannon's guessers missed most often at the beginnings of words. In 1990, Jeffrey Elman saw the same in a network trained to predict the next letter of text with no spaces: its error was high at each word's first letter, and fell as the word went on.
loss/total: The loss for the whole text, L, adds up every step's: two point three four.
loss/sum: In symbols, L is the sum, over the steps t, of minus ln p t, at y t: at each step, minus the log of the probability it gave its target.
loss/mean: Divide by the four steps for the average: about zero point five nine a step, a number that does not grow just because the text is longer.
